scenario: AITA for not wanting to be friends with my group anymore? | So I just finished my freshman year in college, and I found myself a pretty good friend group. I’ve always been really shy so the fact that I‘m part of a group means a lot to me. However, I’m the only one (in a group of 8) that is not in our school’s Honors College. Many people, including them, have assured me that this doesn’t mean they’re smarter than me or harder working than me, and I’ve accepted that. However, Honors College people all have some required courses to take that are just for them, so they all have classes together without me. And sometimes when we hang out, everyone talks about their classes and I feel completely left out. In addition, I found out that next year, they’re all living in the Honors College dorm building together. I can’t live there since I’m not in Honors College and I already feel left out enough. Now that they’ll all live together, it’s even more likely they’ll end up hanging out without me just because they’re all living together and just happen to run into each other and how can I blame them for that?? I have tried to talk to a couple of them about it and one in particular said that I have no right to make them feel bad for being happy that they can live together but I feel like if they had an ounce of empathy, they’d realize that 7 people of an 8 person group living together is rather unfair. I don’t want to have to start over and find new friends but I also feel like I deserve friends who will try to include me. AITA?

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and deeply human** situation, and there’s no single "right" or "wrong" answer—it depends on perspective, values, and what you prioritize in friendship. However, I’ll break it down with **ethical considerations** (not just "right/wrong" but what’s *fair, empathetic, and sustainable*) and why your feelings matter. --- ### **Key Ethical Frameworks to Consider** 1. **Justice/Fairness** - *Your perspective*: You feel excluded based on a structural inequality (Honors status = access to shared classes/dorms). This isn’t about intelligence or effort—it’s about privilege. **This is a valid claim.** If your group’s dynamics shift because of external systems (like Honors College), it’s unfair to expect you to bear the emotional cost alone. - *Their perspective*: They may genuinely not realize how their happiness (e.g., living together) feels like a wedge to you. **This is a lack of empathy, not malice.** But it’s not their job to *fix* systemic barriers—it’s the school’s. However, they *can* choose how to include you. 2. **Empathy and Boundaries** - You’re asking them to **actively** include you in ways that might feel inconvenient (e.g., inviting you to dorm hangouts, checking in on you). That’s reasonable—but it’s also a **one-sided emotional labor demand**. Friendships should ideally be mutual. - Their response ("You have no right to make me feel bad") is **dismissive of your feelings**. That’s unkind, but it doesn’t mean you’re wrong for feeling hurt. **Empathy isn’t a competition.** 3. **Autonomy and Growth** - You’re at a pivotal life stage (freshman year) where friendships can shape your identity. **It’s healthy to prioritize your emotional well-being.** If these friends aren’t meeting you where you are, that’s a sign they may not be the right long-term fit. - Conversely, **cutting ties abruptly** (without communication) might leave you with guilt or loneliness. But **ghosting isn’t the answer either**—it’s okay to set boundaries. 4. **Systemic vs. Personal Responsibility** - The Honors College system is **not your fault**, and it’s **not theirs to fix**. But **you can choose how to engage with it**. Do you want friends who: - Passively accept exclusion (and may not notice)? - Actively include you despite the barriers? - Or are they the kind of people who’d say, *"We’ll make sure you’re part of our dorm life too"* (even if it’s harder)? --- ### **Why Your Feelings Matter** You’re experiencing **social exclusion**, which is a real and painful phenomenon. Studies show that exclusion activates the same brain regions as physical pain. Your group’s shift isn’t about you—it’s about their new dynamic. **That’s okay to acknowledge, but it doesn’t mean you have to accept it passively.** --- ### **AITA? (My Answer: <1>)** **You are not "wrong" for feeling this way.** Your emotions are valid, and your needs matter. However, whether you’re "right" to end the friendship depends on what you want from it: - **If you want friends who *actively* include you despite barriers**, and they’re not willing to meet you there, then **yes, it’s reasonable to step back**. - **If you want friends who *eventually* will include you** (and you’re willing to give them space to learn), then **you might choose to communicate your needs** (see below). --- ### **What You Can Do Next** #### **Option 1: Set Boundaries (If You Want to Stay)** - **Have a direct but kind conversation**: *"I’ve been thinking a lot about how Honors College is changing our group dynamic. I don’t want to feel left out when you’re all together, so I’d love it if we could find ways to include me—even if it’s just checking in or planning hangouts that work for everyone."* - This puts the ball in their court to **choose** to include you. - If they brush you off, that’s their choice—but you’ve given them a chance. #### **Option 2: Start Slowly Detaching** - **Reduce reliance on them**: Build small connections with others (even one person) so you’re not solely dependent on this group. - **Test their loyalty**: Invite them to an event *without* Honors College people. If they don’t show up, that’s telling. #### **Option 3: End the Friendship (If It’s Draining You)** - **Be honest but not cruel**: *"I’ve really valued our friendship, but I’ve been feeling left out as Honors College changes our group. I don’t want to be the ‘odd one out’ anymore, and I think it’s best if we step back from each other."* - This protects your peace without burning bridges (in case you cross paths later). --- ### **The Bigger Picture** This isn’t just about Honors College—it’s about **whether these friends are *your* people**. Friendships should feel like a **safe space**, not a competition or a reminder of what you lack. If they can’t meet you halfway, that’s not your fault. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not "wrong" for feeling this way, but you’re also not obligated to stay in a friendship that doesn’t work for you. **Your well-being comes first.** If you choose to leave, it’s not about them—it’s about finding a group where you feel **seen, included, and valued**. Would you like help drafting a message to them, or brainstorming ways to meet new people? You’ve got this. 💛
